hook.text: The data never stops arriving. Clicks, payments, sensor readings: the stream has no last row to wait for. Streaming interviews test how Kafka, a distributed log, spreads it across machines, what a delivery guarantee really promises, and how to count over time when events arrive late and out of order.

plan.text: Fifteen questions: twelve worked through, most on one small stream of the video's own, twelve clicks from four users, then three quick ones.

topic.text: Question one. What are Kafka topics, partitions, and offsets?

topic-log.text: A topic is a named log that only grows at its end. It's split into partitions, the unit of parallelism. Each message gets an offset: its position in its partition, counting up from zero.

topic-key.text: The producer hashes each message's key to pick a partition, so all of ava's clicks land in one, in the order they arrived. Order holds inside a partition, never across them. A message with no key goes round-robin.

parts.text: Question two. Why does the number of partitions matter in Kafka?

parts-cap.text: Partitions cap how many consumers can share the work, and set where order holds. More of them buy throughput, at a cost: more open files, longer rebalances, more latency.

parts-move.text: You can add partitions later but never remove them, and adding them moves keys. Model it with ten thousand keys, hashed into three partitions, then four: seventy-four percent move, so a user's new clicks can be read before their old ones. Size for peak, with headroom.

group.text: Question three. What is a consumer group, and how does it scale consumption?

group-def.text: A consumer group is a set of consumers that read one topic together. Each partition goes to exactly one of them, so the work is split and nothing is read twice.

group-scale.text: Two consumers share three partitions. Add a third, and the group rebalances: one partition each. Add a fourth, and it sits idle. Parallelism stops at the partition count.

group-fan.text: A second group gets every message again, on its own: that's how one stream feeds several pipelines.

commit.text: Question four. What are consumer offsets and why commit them?

commit-def.text: A commit records how far the group has processed each partition, and Kafka stores it. After a crash or a rebalance, the next owner resumes from the last commit, not from the start.

commit-when.text: So when you commit decides what a crash costs.

semantics.text: Question five. What is the difference between at-least-once, at-most-once, and exactly-once?

sem-most.text: Take one batch, offsets five to nine, and a crash just after seven. Commit first, then process, and eight and nine are skipped for good. That's at-most-once: no duplicates, but messages lost.

sem-least.text: Process first, then commit, and after the crash, five to seven run again. That's at-least-once: nothing lost, but duplicates. It's the usual default, though it can't save a message deleted before anyone read it.

sem-exact.text: Exactly-once means each message has one effect on the result. Not that the code runs once: it can run twice, as long as the second run changes nothing.

sem-sim.text: Model it: a thousand messages, committed every fifty, with three crashes. At-most-once loses fifty-four. At-least-once processes ninety-six of them twice.

idem.text: Question six. How do you make a consumer idempotent?

idem-how.text: Make a replay harmless. Upsert by key instead of a blind insert, so a second copy overwrites its row with the same values. Or store each message's id, and skip any you've already seen.

idem-sim.text: In the model, blind inserts leave a thousand and ninety-six rows; the idempotent consumer leaves a thousand. That's effectively-once, without a distributed transaction.

eos.text: Question seven. What is exactly-once processing in Kafka, and how is it achieved?

eos-producer.text: Inside Kafka, two pieces. An idempotent producer numbers what it sends, with a producer id and a sequence number, so the broker drops a retried copy.

eos-txn.text: And a transaction writes the output messages and the consumer's offsets together: both land, or neither does. That's the consume, transform, produce loop.

eos-edge.text: The guarantee stops at Kafka's edge. An email, an API call or an outside database isn't in the transaction, so each has to join it, or accept idempotent writes.

time.text: Question eight. What is event time versus processing time?

time-def.text: Event time is when it happened, stamped in the event. Processing time is when the engine handles it. Network delay, retries, a phone that was offline, batched uploads: each pulls the two apart.

time-count.text: Here are the twelve clicks, placed at both. Count them per ten seconds by arrival, and dee's click from second eight lands in the wrong window: four, then five. By event time it's five, then four. Correct counts use event time.

wm.text: Question nine. What is a watermark?

wm-def.text: A watermark is the engine's estimate that every event before some time has arrived, so it can close a window and emit it. A common rule: the latest event time seen, minus an allowed delay. It's progress, not proof: an older event can still turn up.

wm-three.text: Allow three seconds, and the first window closes at thirteen and a half seconds, with four clicks. Then dee's click arrives behind a watermark at twelve: it's late.

wm-ten.text: Allow ten, and it counts, but the window closes almost eight seconds later. A longer delay buys completeness with latency, and holds more state.

late.text: Question ten. How do you handle late-arriving data?

late-fix.text: Combine three things. Keep a window's state for an allowed lateness past the watermark, and update its result when a late event arrives: four becomes five. Send anything later to a side output, not into silence. And have the sink upsert, so the correction replaces the row instead of adding one.

late-trig.text: Some engines emit early, on-time and late results for one window. How late data gets, and how much it matters, decides the mix.

windows.text: Question eleven. What is windowing, and what are the main window types?

win-def.text: Windowing cuts an endless stream into finite buckets you can aggregate.

win-tumble.text: Tumbling windows are fixed and never overlap. Ten seconds each, so every click lands in exactly one: five, four, three.

win-slide.text: Sliding windows, also called hopping, are fixed but overlap. Ten seconds long, starting every five, so each click counts in two.

win-session.text: Session windows have no fixed size: one closes after a gap of inactivity. With a five-second gap, ava's five clicks make two sessions, which is how you sessionize users.

pressure.text: Question twelve. What is backpressure, and how do streaming systems handle it?

bp-def.text: Backpressure is a consumer that can't keep up. Kafka absorbs it: the log is durable, so a slow consumer falls behind and nothing is dropped. Push-based systems push back instead, and slow the producer.

bp-lag.text: Watch consumer lag: the distance from the latest offset to the committed one. Model it: about a hundred messages a second arrive, and one consumer handles eighty. After a minute, lag is over eleven hundred.

bp-fix.text: A second consumer, on a partition of its own, clears it in eighteen seconds. Rising lag means more partitions and consumers, or faster processing.

r-compact.text: Log compaction keeps at least the latest value for each key and clears out older ones, instead of expiring by age. The topic becomes a snapshot of current state, like each user's latest profile, to rebuild state from. It runs alongside time-based retention.

r-join.text: A batch join can wait for every row; a stream join can't, because neither side ends. Stream to stream, it buffers each side's recent events in a time window, matches across them, and lets the watermark expire old state. Stream to table, each event looks up a table kept current, often a compacted topic.

r-dlq.text: And a dead-letter queue catches messages a consumer can't process: malformed, off-schema, or failing again and again. The main stream keeps flowing instead of stalling on one poison message; the bad ones wait to be inspected, fixed and replayed. A batch pipeline sets bad rows or whole tasks aside the same way, so a few don't stop everything, and none vanish.

next.text: Every one of these streams lands somewhere, and how it's stored decides what reading it costs. Next: data warehousing and storage.
